strengths: The paper presents a consolidated set of results on two recently popular natural language planning benchmarks, along with additionally generated problems in PDDL planning domains.

This is the first work that systematically analyzes LLM planning capabilities with fine-tuning on optimal solutions, and if fine-tuning is effective with respect to generalizing across different problem categories under a domain (for example, training on PDDL blocksworld problems with 3-7 blocks and testing with PDDL problems of 8-9 blocks, and so on).
A new NL planning benchmark dataset.

In terms of originality, there are similar benchmarks such as PlanBench available in the literature. The authors argue that the paper also considers many-shot in-context learning settings, as shown in Figure 2. The number of few-shot exemplars ranges from 1 to 400.
Figure 4 shows results from three inference-time ICL methods: ToT, MCTS, and Debate-as-reasoning in non-PDDL-based domains.
Lastly, this paper also shows the experiment results from the fine-tuning setting.
Originality: This paper runs large-scale experiments on environments explored by the LLM planning community using new models.
Quality: This paper has plenty of results that substantiate past findings.
Clarity: The paper is written very clearly.
Significance: Some of the experiments may suggest that newer models deviate from past findings (see questions).
weaknesses: Novelty – The paper only combines existing PDDL planning dataset (PlanBench) and travel planning domains, with the addition of some newly generated test problems, which seems more like packaging the two domains together than presenting a new dataset; the reviewer asks for details such as what percentage of problems are new.

Unjustified evaluations for improved performance – The paper relies on prompt engineering and cherry-picking evaluation data, giving all the benefit of the doubt to LLMs at the expense of human effort; the reviewer suggests noting challenges LLMs face without such human interventions.

Fine-tuning results – Near‑perfect accuracy is shown only when train and eval data consist of similar problem cases, indicating possible over‑fitting and not supporting conclusions about LLM generalization.
Did not find the paper to have novel results (please refer to questions).
No details on how the plans are being generated using FD (which heuristic is being used to generate optimal plans?).
The NL translated prompt does not include PDDL domain, making me question how any LLM is supposed to know all actions, preconditions, and effects for a given domain?

Not a complete coverage of literature on plan generation; authors in [1] introduce thought of search which steers LLMs to solve 100% planning problems, and [2] already provided similar conclusions on SFT using even smaller parameter models and also discussed multiple plan generalization issues.

Coverage of classical planning domains – The three presented domains are over 20 years old, have minimal PDDL features (almost STRIPS with a negative precondition), and the work does not consider coverage of translation of the language.

Quality of translations – The translation is done by hand‑crafted regular expressions rather than natural language, raising doubts about the usefulness of the dataset for enhancing LLM reasoning, and the scale of problems is tiny.
The paper has very little novelty to contribute to the LLM planning community since it reproduces many results and echoes insights that have been communicated in other papers.
The three key findings on plan generalization presented in the conclusion are not new and have already been discussed in prior work such as [12].
It is unclear why the paper introduces five datasets but only experiments on subsets (mainly Blocksworld and Logistics), leaving the purpose of the other datasets ambiguous.
